story_text.value:
If you're following the photopea incident, I'm sure you'd concur that the writing was on the wall. It's an inevitable outcome of the rise of AI in software dev. Any project that sees a semblance of success will be cloned overnight many times over and will find itself competing with its own copies.

We saw glimpses of a similar situation in the past when large cloud platforms cloned popular softwares in a not a very dissimilar manner. This led to the creation of "source available" as an alternative to open source that gained some traction of its own. But since this mostly affected a few large players, open source by and itself was large unaffected still supported by large volumes of individuals driven by passion, motivated towards their craft.

The concept of open source is itself something of an anomaly not seen in any other industry or at any other time in history. Partly fueled by an individual's desire to exhibit original work, and partly supported by the fact that code needs someone of an equal to work with, it still allowed authors to reap a net benefit while giving out their IP for free. LLMs have turned that picture over completely. It's not only trivial to derive, for all purposes, an exact copy of the IP while obscuring the source, it's also possible to maintain and operate the IP with a relatively low bar of expertise. But the other inconspicuous problem brought about by LLMs is that can you even claim original work any more? When no one believes that you wrote it yourself, what motivation remains to continue publishing as open source? With no net benefit to revealing your IP, will we see a revival to closed source distribution again?

title.value: Ask HN: Is this the beginning of the end of open source?

story_text.value:
Hi, I built acceptodds, a prediction market on conference peer review. Every ICLR 2027 submission (42k papers) has a market: Accept vs. Reject.

Like many in the ML community, I think the current conference/paper situation is a bit broken. I'm not sure how to fix it, but this is my attempt at building something fun to get the conversation started.

Some details: - Prices come from Hanson's LMSR (logarithmic market scoring rule).

- You can sell and/or rebuy at any time

- There's a public leaderboard that ranks traders by P&L.

- It uses an in-app currency called reputation. It can't be converted to money.

- Bots can trade too, and they're encouraged. If you can get an LLM to predict the market, that would be cool! There's a public HTTP API with an OpenAPI spec (/api/v1/openapi.json).

- Comments are pseudonymous, like on OpenReview ("User k3xm"), but they show the author's position.

- There's also a 2D map of all submissions: https://acceptodds.com/map

How would you extend this? How should ML conference reviews work? Is there something better than open review?

Go find your own paper (if you have one), place a bet and LMK what you think :)

title.value: Show HN: Acceptodds a prediction market on which ICLR 2027 papers get accepted

story_text.value: I got recently laid off and wanted to learn and play with tools that are popular today as an exercise. Homebrew has some interesting analytics, but it only provides snapshots, you don't have a feel how the popularity of competing tools and technologies changed over time. So I started to take weekly snapshots of the last 30 days data of both formulas and casks. While I had some initial success with clustering packages based on their descriptions, but so far I wouldn't leave it on autopilot. However it serves as a reasonable basis for manual curation. I'd appreciate ideas on how to improve identifying packages of the same domain. (https://github.com/greg76/toth) One of the first surprises for me was that how Codex has been gaining momentum for the last two months compared to Claude Code. Also, while I was looking into the data rolling in, the drop of downloads across the board looked suspicious. I have reached out to the homebrew team and they confirmed that 7.0.0 introduced a regression in analytics reporting and with a sameday fix 7.0.6 should be reporting data as before.

story_text.value:
Huge open source projects have been successful by building upon dozens to hundreds of small libraries that encapsulate functionality and complexity.

AI coding uses these libraries to quickly build applications.

With the latest round of model releases I am seeing that AI can now generate the functionality of almost any library in-line as it generates the application.

When building took a long time, breaking things down into well defined modules, shipping incrementally, and reusing code, were essential techniques. They seem much less important when AI is doing the work.

Is software library creation obsolete?

title.value: Is library building obsoleted by AI coding?

story_text.value:
Hi there.

I used to work in international trade, and encountered many situations where people create a PDF from a system, send it to another party, and the other party parses the PDF to input into their system.

As AI agents become first principles to deal with the documents, I believe the extra document creation and parsing step will become unnecessary.

So I created a JSON viewer, where you can sign JSON and send it to other parties as a portable document. It can also display JSON data in a more document-like format.

I’m wondering if such a format can be used as a replacement for some document communication today. I'd be so happy to hear your thoughts.

story_text.value:
In 2019, I was teaching science at an international school in Chiang Mai. One day before class, one of my Grade 7 students asked me about flat earth. He had heard the idea from Kyrie Irving and then spent the night on flat earth sites.

We walked through the claims and I explained why those arguments failed. He listened with interest. I was glad he'd come to me. He hadn't made up his mind yet; he was just curious. But this made me wonder if teaching the course content I was teaching was enough.

To be clear: I do think teaching facts is important. For example, when students learn about gravity, physics, and space, they're better prepared to see why flat earth arguments are wrong. The problem is we can't teach facts fast enough to combat the wide variety of misinformation and manipulation kids face on the internet every day.

This is what got me thinking that kids need to learn how to evaluate claims and information across a wide range of topics. While we can't prepare them for every false or misleading claim they might encounter, we can give them tools to assess them.

That eventually led my husband and I to build Critikid, a site for teaching kids and teens. We've been working on it for 3 years now! He does the technical work (design and coding) and I do the educational content creation.

By now, there are 5 interactive courses for ages 5-18 on logical fallacies, media literacy, emotional intelligence, statistical reasoning, and formal logic. There are also worksheets and lesson plans.

I often teach through stories, as stories make abstract critical thinking concepts concrete (and they're fun!)

If you'd like to try it, all of the courses have a free first lesson.

Are there any other topics that you think should be included in kids' critical thinking education that I've missed?

title.value: Show HN: A critical thinking site for kids and teens

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

Some friends and I built an app called Sidekick that joins your telehealth visits in real-time. It explains medical terms and suggests useful questions, including ones you may not have thought to ask. After the visit, it provides a summary including next steps, so you can focus on the conversation instead of taking notes.

The idea of Sidekick came from our team's experiences with healthcare. Our founder, Rahul, had stage three cancer at 17. His mom had to manage everything around his care: taking notes through treatment, figuring out what questions to ask, etc. A decade later and he’s now in remission, but still sees a lot of specialists and deals with the same challenges.

Another teammate became a caregiver after his dad had a severe stroke. He found himself taking notes, looking up medical terms, and trying to keep track of what was said during every doctor visit. Others have dealt with situations like this when navigating pancreatitis and other serious health issues.

These experiences got us interested in how we might be able to reduce the burden on the patient or caregiver.

A lot of products focus on simply recording or summarizing the visit. That's useful and a step in the right direction, but we kept coming back to the fact that a lot of the challenge originates while the conversation is still happening. If you can catch something in the moment, you can address it with your clinician immediately and potentially lead to better outcomes. If you realize you missed something after the visit, then you have to try to get another appointment (and in SF I often can't get another doctor visit till 2 months later).

So we built Sidekick, to help patients and caregivers during a visit in real-time to translate medical jargon and suggest useful questions, ideally without becoming a distraction.

If you want to try it, you can download it on our website. Sidekick is desktop-only for now, but we’re working on a mobile app for in-person visits.

We would be especially interested to hear feedback on the live part of the experience. What are your thoughts on the balance between live help vs after-visit? Would something pre-visit be more helpful?

title.value: Show HN: We built a real-time desktop companion for patient's telehealth visits

If you want to try it, you can download it on our website. Sidekick is desktop-only for now, but we’re working on a mobile app for in-person visits.

We would be especially interested to hear feedback on the live part of the experience. What are your thoughts on the balance between live help vs after-visit? Would something pre-visit be more helpful?
hits.title: Show HN: We built a real-time desktop companion for patient's telehealth visits

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Mark. Companies are really pushing cloud agents, but I found myself wanting to run agents on my Mac off-hours on my existing Claude/Codex subs.

I'd hit my usage limit coding with Fable, but not my limit on other models for tasks like marketing, research and content creation. So I built an orchestrator that organizes my agents into departments (or ships) where they have overriding goals/milestones and a "captain" agent can spawn other agents working in that department.

I think this structure works better than individual agent workers in an office. (Mundler Difflin)

The user can prompt the agent dispatcher for one-off or recurring tasks, which can be controlled from a Slack or a Telegram bot. Since Overboard has context about all your local projects it knows where it should spawn an agent. You can also talk to department heads or the main agent to see what human blockers are stalling projects, or give new direction for a department. Would love to hear feedback about the project. It's not open-source but there is a 14 day trial so anyone can test if it's useful before buying a license. (one-time $49)

story_text.value:
Light it up with Hypercolor, a new RGB lighting orchestration platform for all platforms and all devices. Effects are web pages (or glsl), rendered by an internal browser GPU accelerated all the way to the pixels. It's pure rust from the Servo renderer to the WASM UI.

Comes with 40+ effects, supports ambilight, display faces, system monitoring, screen casting, and audio. Device support is pretty good but it's early and this is where we need the most help! You can find the full support matrix on the site, and there is also an OpenRGB bridge as a fallback. There's support for a few unique devices too like the Ableton Push 2 and ROLI Blocks. My favorite thing about this engine is the ability to create multiple effect zones and manage them independently! My whole house runs on it now. It's Apache licensed, and a cloud service is coming with remote and smart home support. A Home Assistant integration is already available.

The best way to set up Hypercolor is to just have an agent do it for you using the bundled skill. Just describe your setup, case type, hardware, etc, and it will find all the specs and configure it for you. Or just do it the good old-fashioned way in Studio!

Please check it out and file and issue if you're looking for device support. I can only build drivers for devices I have access too, please open PRs if you're able to contribute! Agents can reverse engineer your hardware and build a driver easily, if you want to go that route (the repo is designed for agents). We have a full TypeScript effects SDK for easy effect creation too, and support existing Lightscript based html effects out of the box.

I've had a lot of fun building this and I hope you enjoy it!

Hey yall! I needed a way to cap my own phone use so downloaded one of the many "do pushups to unlock your phone apps". I loved it! ios/android supported!

Really confused between React Native and Flutter. I’ve mostly worked with Flutter and a little bit with React Native, but that was quite a while back, so I’m not sure how things stand today.

I’m building a project with a Node.js + tRPC backend, so React Native is looking really tempting cause of that Typescript.

While researching I've seen mixed reviews about performance in React Native like people saying they've spend weeks finding and managing performance issue which does makes me worry.

The app I wanna build doesn't have complex canvas work or crazy animations. For a typical production app, what’s the performance situation with React Native vs Flutter now? Are there any major concerns which I should know before looking in React Native?

story_text.value:
A year ago, I came across Google Notebook LM. I was completely blown away at the time: it wasn't just a ChatGPT-style conversation, but rather introduced an "input—conversation—output" model, turning itself into a workspace for content creators. However, to use it smoothly required a Google subscription, and I really didn't have spare money in my wallet to subscribe, so I could only consider finding some self-hosted alternatives.

I saw many open-source versions of Notebook LM on GitHub, the most famous being lfnovo/open-notebook, but it requires Docker deployment. To be honest, I hate that everything requires Docker deployment. What I need is to click an icon and open it for use, rather than racking my brains to modify someone else's Docker Compose template to run a simple piece of software, while also consuming a large amount of my computer resources.

So I wrote a Notebook LM-inspired client based on Electron myself: KnowNote. I published it on X, and the response seemed pretty good. My repository's star count soared. This was my first open-source project, and it excited me immensely. I developed all the fancy features by following Notebook LM's functionality exactly—mind maps, flashcards, quizzes, and so on—hoping to truly bring Notebook LM locally.

But later everything began to change. Many comments under my X posts said: "Isn't this just reinventing the wheel?"; the GitHub star count stopped growing; a large number of boring and low-quality PRs flooded the entire repository. I was at a loss all of a sudden, became lazy, and the repository stopped being updated for nearly a year.

Recently, I calmed my mindset and truly began to look at the problem from a product manager's perspective. I went through many discussions on Reddit and X about Notebook LM and its derivatives, and found that everyone's mindset and the topics they focused on had also begun to shift: at first everyone was praising how excellent Notebook LM was, but now they were discussing "What do you actually use NotebookLM for?" "What's the difference between it and just throwing files to ChatGPT / Gemini?" "How can plugins, tools, and other products make it better to use?"

I realized that even Notebook LM cannot satisfy all users' needs. Merely copying it completely will only lead me down its old path. I increasingly feel that KnowNote should not chase after NotebookLM's feature list. I collected the questions everyone cared about most and found that most discussions revolved around this one core issue:

When you find an answer from a large amount of material through AI, how do you make that process more accurate, more transparent, and more comfortable?

It dawned on me that what I should truly solve well is this most core user problem, rather than drifting with the crowd.

In the past few days, I redesigned KnowNote's future roadmap, refocusing on AI Q&A, information retrieval, source citation, and the interactive experience built around these capabilities, using AI for reconstruction. Now I have released version v1.5.0, and I am very happy to reintroduce this project to everyone. Although many things may still not be easy to use, and I myself don't even have answers for many directions, I actually hope even more that more people will come in and give it a try right now. If you have used NotebookLM, Obsidian, various AI knowledge bases, or RAG tools, I especially want to know: What is the most frustrating thing for you when using these products or is there any need you have always wanted but existing products have never solved well?

If you are willing, you can try KnowNote, and you are also welcome to directly submit Issues, complain, or tell me that this direction simply doesn't hold up. Now I want to treat it more as a project that slowly seeks answers together with the community.

GitHub: https://github.com/mrsibe/KnowNote
